articleTitle: Integrated Circuit Fabrication Technology
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: GaAs integrated circuit technology has matured to the point where manufacturability is an important and widespread concern. Several companies have recently announced commercial products and others are offering foundry activities. These efforts are summarized in this session by two invited papers which survey both linear and digital manufacturing technologies. Another paper offers new insight into a crucial manufacturing issue, the interaction of an anneal cap with the substrate. Finally, the last two papers report recent advances in self-aligned gate processes for MESFETs and MODFETs.

articleTitle: Microwave Communications
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Linear MMIC technology is beginning to hoe the road from research oriented demonstrations to potential use in specific system applications. This FET based technology has reached the point where the pacing issues are focused on circuit configurations, their design and their serious application at the subsystems level. However, the path to ultimate success (low cost, high performance, reliability) is lined with obstacles related to design philosophy, CAD software limitations and device modeling. These areas must be revisited and refined in order to meet stringent MMIC design specifications.

articleTitle: Digital Integrated Circuits (II)
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Rapid progress is being made in the development of LSI-III-V ICs as well as very high performance novel device structures. This session highlights the advances made in LSI GaAs represented by achieving levels of complexity to realize 8×8 multipliers and SRAMs of 16K bit complexity. Ultra high speed heterojunction structures have been made demonstrating performance up to 10 GHz.

articleTitle: Radiation Effects
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: GaAs based integrated circuits are particularly suited for use in applications that have very high radiation tolerance requirements. GaAs devices and integrated circuits are known to survive total ionizing radiation doses that are orders of magnitude higher than can be tolerated by silicon based components.

articleTitle: Digital Integrated Circuits (I)
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: This session begins with a 40 gate circuit comparison of silicon NMOS versus LP BFL technologies highlighting not only the speed advantages of GaAs but also the significant power reductions for GaAs when operated at the slower silicon speed levels.

articleTitle: Materials
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The understanding and characterization of materials continues to be of concern for the fabrication of quality integrated circuits with high yield. MBE materials for HEMT circuits are reviewed in the invited talk which highlights-the important material considerations for the implementation of this technology. The use of semi- insulating GaAs substrates is prevalent in the more conventional MESFET technology. The promise of more uniform FET Characteristics due to improved crystal growth conditions and reduced dislocation densities offer great potential for much higher yield of integrated circuits.

articleTitle: Packaging
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Full utilization of the performance capabilities of GaAs integrated circuits requires an appropriate packaging technology. These papers address this important issue and describe specific packages. One paper proposes a design applicable to both monolithic microwave and digital circuits. The other two address the design for digital circuits operating at frequencies of several gigaherz.

articleTitle: Broadband Linear Integrated Circuits
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Multi-octave bandwidths are now being achieved by GaAs MMICs. These extreme bandwidths are made possible by a unique feature of monolithic integration—individual FET cells can be connected directly to passive circuit elements without intervening bond pads and wires. This session shows how distributed traveling wave techniques, feedback techniques, and broadband switch designs are being used to achieve bandwidth as great as 28 GHz. In addition, enhanced performance of filters and television tuners using GaAs ICs is shown.

articleTitle: Processing Technologies for GaAs Memory LSIs
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A 16 Kb GaAs static random access memory (SRAM) has been designed adopting direct coupled FET logic (DCFL) circuitry for the main and has been fabricated using self-aligned MESFETs with Self-Aligned Implantation for Ν<sup>+</sup> -layer Technology (SAINT). This SRAM consists of more than 10<sup>5</sup> FETs, the largest integrated scale m GaAs ICs. A minimum address access time of 4.1 ns has been achieved with a total power dissipation of 2.52 W.

articleTitle: Application of Heterojunction Bipolar Transistors to High Speed, Small-Scale Digital Integrated Circuits
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The fabrication and performance of a number of small-scale (20-60 transistors) integrated circuits based on GaAs/(Ga,Al )As heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) in an emitter-coupled logic approach are described. The circuits include ring oscillators, with propagation delay times down to 40 pS in current-mode logic gates; frequency dividers, operating with input frequencies up to 8.5 GHz; and a 4-bit pattern generator, operating with clock frequencies up to more than 2 GHz (data rates of 4-Gbit/s in nonreturn-to-zero format). Initial results of transistor uniformity and circuit yield are shown to be excellent.

articleTitle: Ultra High Speed Integrated Circuits with Selectively Doped Heterostructure Transistors
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: We report on the performance of ring oscillators and frequency dividers made with SDHTs (Selectively Doped Heterostructure Transistors). Ring oscillators with submicron driver transistor gates have been fabricated using direct e-beam writing. A minimum propagation delay of 11.0 ps was obtained with 0.4 μm gates at 77 K. The speed-power product was 15.0 fJ/gate at 1.1 V bias. A dual-clocked M/S (master/slave) flip-flop frequency divider using 1 Mm dual-gate SDHTs was also fabricated and tested. This is the first implementation of a DCFL circuit with NAND-type logic gates. A maximum dividing frequency of 5.5 (10.1) GHz was achieved at 300 (77) K. Both the 11.0 ps/gate ring oscillator delay and the 10.1 GHz dividing frequency represent the fastest speed reported for such semiconductor circuits.

articleTitle: Gamma Ray Radiation Effects on Mmic’s Elements
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Three experimental studies concerning-radiation effects of gamma ray on GaAs MMIC's elements are reported. Firstly, the effects of gamma ray on passive elements such as MIM capacitors and SBDs are discussed. No significant change has been observed for these elements up to 10<sup>8</sup> rads. Secondly, performance of GaAs FETs heated at 200 °C is monitored during gamma ray irradiation up to 10<sup>9</sup> rads. The smaller change in DC parameters has been observed comparing to samples without heating. No annealing effects have been observed for the samples irradiated at high temperature. Finally, degradation of Au/Ni/AuGe ohmic electrodes caused by gamma ray irradiation up to 10<sup>9</sup> rads in various ambient gases is discussed. It has been clarified that H<inf>2</inf>O plays an important role in the enhancement of the inter-diffusion among the ohmic metal layers.

articleTitle: Cross-Talk Predictions and Reducing Techniques for High Speed GaAs Digital ICs
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Analyzing and predicting high speed digital signal transmission properties in GaAs integrated circuits are presented, and a cross-talk noise reduction method is proposed on the basis of simulated results. The transmitted signal and the cross-talk noise wave form have been simulated by the developed time domain strong coupling transmission line analysis program. Cross-talk noises in GaAs have been found to be minimized by a low dielectric constant interlayer between the GaAs wafer and lines according to some calculated results. Some experimental data, using ceramic substrates instead of GaAs wafers, agreed with the predicted data.

articleTitle: Direct Experimental Comparison of Submicron GaAs and Si NMOS MSI Digital IC's
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Scaling down of GaAs and Si NMOS digital IC' s (1) has raised the question of the real advantage of GaAs over Si for low power (P ≤ 1 mW/gate), high speed applications (tpd ≤ 200 ps/gate for F/O = 3). So far comparisons have been either theoretical (2) or based on different designs with different design rules. In order to make a useful comparison, the same MSI finite-state machine has been fabricated (3), using a LPBFL approach for the GaAs circuit and NMOS for the silicon one. This circuit is a 3 bit feed-back adder with combinational and sequential blocks. The main experimental results show that GaAs LPBFL is about twice as fast as Si NMOS for 1 mW/gate with Lch = 0.6 µm (channel length) and 2 µm design rules. Moreover, GaAs LPBFL is about 8 times less power consuming than Si NMOS for 250 ps tpd/gate (FO = 3).

articleTitle: A Gallium Arsenide Configurable Cell Array using Buffered FET Logic
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A GaAs configurable cell array has been fabricated using 1 µm gate MESFETs on 3 inch GaAs substrates. Depletion-mode MESFETs configured in BFL structures were used to implement the logic cells. The cells are programmable for several logic functions. Placement and routing software was developed. Measured results on several cell configurations with various device sizes yielded speed-power products ranging from 162 fJ to 460 fJ. A 306 cell array (equivalent to approximately 430 NOR gates) occupying a chip area of 2.0 mm × 2.8 mm was fabricated. A 5 × 5 bit parallel multiplier implemented with this array showed a multiplication time of 6.5 nsec, and a power dissipation ranging from 337 mW to 722 mW corresponding to a cell power of 1.30 mW/cell to 2.79 mW/cell. The development of a cell array containing 732 cells implementing an 8 × 8 multiplier is discussed.

articleTitle: GaAs Technology for High Speed A/D Converters
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: GaAs analog-to-digital converters, ADCs, have the potential for significantly higher conversion speed than Si ADCs. However, critical issues in materials, processing and design must be resolved before this performance potential is realized. In this paper we summarize the technological difficulties, outline potential solutions and predict the performance of high speed GaAs ADCs. Our work establishes the feasibility of real-time analog-to-digital conversion at gigasample per second rates and points out the technological improvements which must be made.

articleTitle: Survey of Manufacturing Capabilities for GaAs Digital Integrated Circuits
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: GaAs microwave circuits can be found in a number of prototype systems, yet there exists no manufacturing capability for GaAs based components to which a silicon IC producer would deem to give even pilot line status. Until very recently one could not place a purchase order for any GaAs components more complex than a single transistor and these were designed for microwave applications. Digital GaAs technologies have been strictly research curiosities; supported primarily by Government contract or IR&D funds. The need for GaAs components at X-band and above is well recognized. Why hasn't this need for microwave components spawned a GaAs manufacturing capability that could produce digital LSI circuits now that the need for such circuits is emerging in a variety of DoD's future systems? A ready answer was provided in one of the responses received to the questionnaire on Manufacturing Capabilities for GaAs Digital Integrated Circuits - the market character for digital and analog circuits is very different (Table 1). It thus is appropriate that the manufacturing problems of digital and analog GaAs IC be treated as separate topics that may, at best, have a peripheral influence on each other.

articleTitle: MBE Materials Considerations for HEMT Circuits
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: MBE materials requirements for HEMT circuits now and in the near future are considered. The epitaxial structures required for optimum device and circuit performance are outlined and evaluated in terms of the relative degree of difficulty for the MBE process. Methods for improving HEMT devices and circuits by engineering better epitaxial structures are discussed. Similarly, considerations of wafer uniformity, reproducibility, and defect densities are reviewed. The incremental cost of adding MBE capabilities to a GaAs pilot line in order to produce HEMT circuits is investigated, and MOCVD as an alternate epitaxial technique is considered. It is concluded that HEMT structures can be grown by MBE in sufficient quantity for pilot production. Yield of good wafers will be determined by MBE reproducibility and oval defect densities.

articleTitle: A Low Power Gigabit IC Fabrication Technology
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A self-aligned gate MESFET IC process using refractory metal-sil icon gates has been developed for LSI circuits at gigabit speeds. It includes two levels of low resistance (<.07 ohm/sq.) metalization patterned using a dielectric assisted liftoff process. A 4 micron pitch is achieved with adjacent vias allowed. Transconductances as high as 216 mS/mm are obtained for 0.7 micron gates and 170 mS/mm for 1 micron gates with corresponding output conductance of 8 mS/mm. Typical threshold voltage variations across a three inch wafer are 50-70 mV with short range (1.0 mm × 0.6 mm) uniformity about 20 mV and as low as 10 mV. Osing this process, divide-by-four circuits designed for 500 MHz and operating up to 2.5 GHz have been fabricated with gate power dissipation of .172 mW/gate at a 1 GHz clock frequency.

articleTitle: X-Band Low-Noise GaAs Monolithic Frequency Converter
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: An X-band low-noise GaAs monolithic frequency converter has been developed. The frequency converter consists of an X-band low-noise amplifier, an image rejection filter, an X-band dual gate FET mixer and an IF-band buffer amplifier. The chip size is 3.4 × 1.5 mm. The design considerations, fabrication and microwave performances for the frequency converter are described. Less than 3-dB noise figure and more than 34-dB conversion gain were obtained.

articleTitle: Threshold Voltage Uniformity of Mesfets Fabricated on GaAs and in-Alloyed GaAs Substrates
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The uniformity of threshold voltage (V<inf>th</inf>) for planar MESFETs has been investigated as a function of (1) starting substrate material type (both undoped LEC GaAs and In-alloyed GaAs), (2) dislocation density and FET-to-dislocati on distance and (3) process related parameters. A whole wafer FET array was used to map both full 2" diameter wafer V<inf>th</inf> uniformity as well as short range (≈1 mm × 1 mm) uniformity. Major results show no correlation of FET threshold voltage with proximity to a dislocation. However, average threshold voltage shifts are observed for high dislocation density regions. Best threshold uniformity to date has been obtained on indium-alloyed LEC GaAs which has large regions of nearly-zero dislocation density. Post-growth annealing of conventional LEC GaAs appears to offer some uniformity enhancement over as-grown material. Best uniformity achieved to date is 8.5 mV standard deviation (S.D.) in threshold voltage for 48 FETs distributed over a 1 mm<sup>2</sup> area and 35 mV S.D. across a 2" wafer. These results point to substrate improvements which will enhance parametric yield in future GaAs LSI and VLSI circuits and A/D converters where utmost device uniformity is essential.

articleTitle: Waffleline - A Packaging Technique for Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: WAFFLELINE, a high density packaging technique designed for monolithic microwave integrated circuits, is described. WAFFLELINE has been tested at frequencies up to 18 GHz, showing a standing wave ratio of 1.1:1 and signal isolation of crossover wires of greater than 30 dB. Adjacent signal wires, which are separated by 0.050 inches, have greater than 50 dB isolation. This low coupling, high density environment makes WAFFLELINE ideal for high speed monolithic applications.

articleTitle: Broadband GaAs Monolithic Low Noise Amplifiers and Switches for L-Band
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: An 800 MHz-1800 MHz two stage low noise feedback amplifier and a high performance SPDT switch have been developed as general purpose ICs. A gain of 19 ± 1.2 dB and a noise figure of 3.0 dB have been measured for the amplifier chips. An insertion loss of 1 dB with 20 dB off isolation has been measured for the switch chip. Full RF and DC bias circuitry is included on the chips. A novel IC package has been designed based on a leadless chip carrier for surface mounting onto a thick film substrate.

articleTitle: Effects of Melt Composition on Electrical Uniformity of Si Implanted, Undoped, Semi-Insulating GaAs
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The variations of carrier profiles in Si implanted layers were investigated for undoped, semi-insulating GaAs grown from different melt compositions (x=As/(Ga+As)). The activation efficiency was found to increase as the crystals became As rich. The carrier profile uniformity of the implanted layer across the wafers was also found to depend on the melt composition. The most uniform distribution of carrier profiles was obtained for GaAs ingots grown from a melt of slightly As-rich composition (x=0.502 to 0.505). These results demonstrate the importance of stoichiometry control in obtaining electrically uniform Si-implanted layers.

articleTitle: Packages for Ultra-High Speed GaAs ICs
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Two, 36-pin, chip-carrier packages are reported which meet the requirements of ultra-high-speed GaAs ICs with up to 3GHz clock rates and 100 picoseconds rise and fall times. The packaging requirements are analyzed on the basis of propagation delay, stub lengths, cross-talk and power supply regulation. Two packages with internal groundplane, power-supply by-pass capacitors and a maximum package dimensions of 1cm × 1cm are developed. The first packaging approach is based on a multilayer co-fired ceramic technology, whereas, the second approach utilizes a silicon IC as a chip-carrier upon which the GaAs IC die is mounted. In the later case the Si-chip provides shielded transmission lines, power supply regulation, terminating and damping resistors as well as lowers the thermal resistance of the package.

articleTitle: 28 GHz-Band GaAs Monolithic Amplifiers
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A medium power 28GHz-band GaAs monolithic amplifiers have been developed for use in Ka-Band microwave links.FET's 0.4um gate patterns, which contain ten 125um-wide fingers, are formed by variable-shaped electron-beam direct writing with a PMMA film on a spin coated SiO<inf>2</inf> / a buffer resist layer. The amplifier provides a 3.7dB linear gain and a 21.1dBm output power, when the gain is ldB compressed at 28GHz. The frequency band, where the linear gain is more than 3dB, is from 27.7 to 28.9GHz. Chip size is 1×1.3×0.15<sup>t</sup> mm.

articleTitle: Distributed, TraveliΝG Wave Monolithic Amplifiers
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The concept of the distributed or traveling wave amplifier has been known since 1937 [1]. Its first practical implementation appeared in 1948 and was, of course, of vacuum tube design [2]. The efficacy of the distributed approach is in substituting the input and output capacitance of the active device for the capacitance in the L-C lumped element model of the ideal transmission line. Although the parasitic shunt capacitance of a microwave FET is considerably less than that of a vacuum tube, it was inevitable that even the small parasitic capacitance of the FET would eventually hinder amplifier performance. The first distributed amplxfers to use high performance FETS have only recently appeared [3, 4], and their superlative performance has inspired much other work in the field. Their construction consists of an input and an output transmission line coupled by FET devices spaced uniformly along the transmission lines. The input transmission line is periodically loaded by the FET input capacitance and is terminated in its characteristic impedance. The output line is similarly loaded by the FET output capacitance which is insufficient to equalize characteristic impedance and velocity; additional shunt capacitance is usually required. Since device capacitance is effectively and distributati vely incorporated into the transmission lime along its length, it no longer dominates amplifier frequency limitations. The device capacitance and its distributed "lumpiness" along the transmission line can, however, lower the cutoff frequency of the distributed amplifier below that of the classical cutoff frequency of a transmission line which is \text{f}_\text{c} \, = \,1\,/\,\left( {\pi \sqrt {\text{LC}} } \right) This lowering of the cutoff frequency arises when too few devices with individually too much input capacitance are positioned too sparsely along a given length of transmission line. Such sparse spacing effectively causes the complex impedance of the transmission line to become imaginary at a frequency below the cutoff given above. This effect encourages the placement of more but smaller FETS along a given length of transmission line, but the advantage is eventually counterbalanced by transmission line losses. The use of FETs with individual input capacitance of less than 90 femtofarads on a 50 ohm input line is adequate for operation into the lower portion of the millimeter wave spectrum. Figure 1 illustrates the typical simplified schematic diagram for such an amplifier. Of importance in this diagram is that both the input and the output lines are RF-terminated in their characteristic impedance in such a manner that neither gate nor drain bias current is shunted to ground and uselessly dissipated in the terminating resistors. Other important considerations for the impedance-terminating/bias networks are (1) that they properly isolate the bias supplies from the RF signals using sufficient isolation such that several stages may be .upplied from a single bias point and (2) that the complex impedances of the networks are capable of providing a match over the entire operating bandwidth of the device to provide for reqUired gain flatness. The absolute value of the terminating resistors has usually proven critical in achieving gain flatness.

articleTitle: Broadband GaAs FET 2 × 1 Switches
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Two monolithic broadband single pole double throw switches employing both series and shunt zero biased GaAs FETs are presented. One switch operates in the 0-20 GHz frequency band with apprxoimately 2 dB insertion loss and 30 dB isolation. The second switch operates from 6-18 GHz with matched input conditions for all combinations of port selection. Both switches have very low DC power dissipation, fast switching speeds and good large signal performance.

articleTitle: A Double-Conversion Broad Band TV-Tuner with GaAs Ics
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: In conventional terrestrial TV tuners single down conversion is applied comprising three tuners in parallel for reception of the TV frequency band (47-860 MHz). As a consequence 12 tunable resonant circuits have to be adjusted manually for good frequency tracking. A monolithic solution, instead, avoids tweaking of the different tuning circuits and reduces the number of components. Both measures are steps to a costeffective approach. In this paper, a double-conversion broad band tuner based on GaAs-ICs is presented. Its gain (20 dB), noise figure (7.5 dB) and in-channel cross modulation (6 mV) correspond to the state-of-the-art of conventional tuners. Based on an analysis of the measured results necessary improvements in off-channel cross-modulation are discussed.

articleTitle: A Monolithic Limiting Amplifier for Microwave FM Receiver Systems
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A high dynamic range limiting amplifier module, which uses monolithic feedback amplifiers as the active gain elements, has been developed for a variety of FM receiver systems. By using Rf feedback to achieve low VSWR and a flat amplitude characteristic, six two-stage amplifier chips were cascaded (single-ended) with an active temperature compensation network and IF filter so that 60 dB of small signal gain could be obtained. The small chip size and circuit simplicity allows the resulting module to be compact, easy to assemble and inexpensive.

articleTitle: ECL-Compatible GaAs SRAM Circuit Technology for High Performance Computer Application
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Novel circuit technology has been developed to realize GaAs SRAM's that will be competent in real system environments. It has also been successfully applied to a 256×4-bit SRAM. The technology includes: 1. An ECL 100K-compatible input buffer circuit, 2. A normally-on type circuit called an FLSC, whose noise margin is 3-times larger than conventional DCFL's, and 3. Bootstrap capacitors in the data-line load circuit and sensing circuitry to enhance load driving capability. These techniques provide a wide Vth tolerance of ±150mV(30) as well as fast access time and Dout rise/fall time. The fabricated 256×4-bit SRAM has a 2.3ns access time for an 800mV ECL-level input signal. The access time is maintained even when the input voltage swing is decreased to 250mV. Dout rise/fall time is 1.2ns in an on-wafer AC test. It is expected to be only 0.7ns with an output load of 50Ω and 10pF.

articleTitle: A GaAs 4K BIT Static Ram with Noemally-on and -OFF Combination Circuit
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A 4096 × 1bit GaAs static RAM with normally-on and -off combination circuit configuration was designed and fabricated. In the design phase, power/speed trade-off was carefully considered. Transfer gates of memory cells, column switches, word line drivers, address buffers and a sense amplifier were constructed using normally-on type circuit to speed up operation, while other parts, such as flip-flops in memory cells and decoder circuits, were realized by normally-off type circuit to save power. The memory cell size was 48um × 67um, and the chip size was 4.40mm × 5.05mm. The measured X-address access time was 2.6 nsec at power dissipation of 1.8 W.

articleTitle: New Device Structure for 4Kb HEMT SRAM
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Self-aligned High Electron Mobility Transistor (HEMT) technology based on selectively doped GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure for LSI circuits is presented. A unique epistructure, associated with gate dry recessing process which is one of the most important technologies for realizing E/D type HEMT DCFL circuits is described. Making the best use of refined gate recess technology, we have successfully fabricated and tested 4Kb HEMT SRAM, with minimum address access time of 2.0 ns at 77K. This is the highest speed ever reported for 4Kb RAMs.

articleTitle: Charge Effects in GaAs Semi-Insulating Substrates due to Pulsed Ionizing Radiation
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Semi-insulating gallium arsenide wafers with N<sup>+</sup> and P<sup>+</sup> contacts have been irradiated with 100 nsec gamma pulses in a dose rate range from 10<sup>9</sup> to 3·10<sup>11</sup> rad(GaAs)/s, and the induced currents at various applied voltages have been measured. The response time is of the order of a few tens of a nanosecond. In some cases, the induced current exhibits a tail lasting many milliseconds or even seconds. This persistent current is traced to hole injection either from a P<sup>+</sup> contact, or else from the chip-to-package bond.

articleTitle: Capacitor Diode FET LOGIC (CDFL) Circuit Approach for GaAs D-Mesfet I C's
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: This paper describes a new circuit design approach for GaAs depletion-mode MESFET digital ICs, capacitor diode-coupled FET logic (CDFL), which is optimized for performance and commercial manufacturaility, while maintaining low power. Manufacturaility is attained by making the circuits quite tolerant to variations in MESFET pinchoff voltage. High performance at low power is achieved by minimizing the current wasted in level shifting and by carefully controlling the internal logic voltage swings to maintain MESFET operation in high f<inf>T</inf> regions. Typical gate operating frequencies are in the dc to 3GHz range with our L<inf>g</inf> = lum, V<inf>p</inf> = -1.0V D-MESFET process. Both the basic CDFL gate structures and the types of ECL-compatible input and output circuits used with CDFL in the GigaBit 10G PicoLogic™ family of GaAs digital circuits will be described.

articleTitle: The Quick-Chip a Depletion Mode Digital/Analog Array
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: An MSI cell array capable of integrating both analog and digital functions has been fabricated using a high yield depletion mode GaAs MESFET technology. The 80 mil square array contains 28 corecells each capable of supporting 2 UFL or BFL gates or 1 latch configuration. The array also contains 24 I/O cells and pads. A library of logic gates, macro-functions and I/O buffers has been demonstrated and enables rapid circuit realization. The structure of the chip and the cells were designed for full CAD support and auto-place and route software is available to efficiently reduce turn-around time. Typical gate delay is 190 ps (FO=FI=3 plus 500 μm of airbridge) at 20 mW/gate, while I/O power ranges between 25 and 50 mW producing a nominal chip power of 2 watts. A high speed package has also been developed that supports 200 ps risetimes for all 24 I/O pads plus provides easy interconnect to a system circuit board.

articleTitle: A GaAs DCFL Chip Set for Multiplex and Demultiplex Applications at Gigabit/Sec Data Rates
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: We report on the development of a family of MSI DCFL GaAs MESFET digital integrated circuits that perform multiplex and demultiplex functions at data rates above 1 Gbit/sec. Circuit architectures include single clocked 6-NOR type D and complementary clocked master slave flip-flops. Circuit complexity ranges from buffered flip-flops, modulus 2, 4 and 12 frequency dividers, parallel and serial registers to fully integrated 12:1 multiplexer and 1:12 demultiplexers. Device fabrication on 2" n<sup>+</sup>/n epitaxy features a 1 μm self-aligned recessed gate structure. Performance measurements for the 6-NOR designs include inpackage operation at 2.0 Gbit/sec clock rate for register and divider circuits and in-wafer operation up to 1.3 Gbit/sec for the 12:1 multiplexer circuits. In addition we have obtained a maximum toggle frequency of 5.6 GHz for the 6-NOR type D modulus 4 divider (7=30010 and a minimum ring oscillator gate delay of 13.7 ps (T=300Κ). Reduced power implementations have shown ring oscillator gate delays of 30.7 ps with an associated speed power product of 4.3 fJ.

articleTitle: GaAs MMICs: Manufacturing Trends and Issues
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The critical issues impacting the manufacturability of GaAs monolithic microwave integrated circuits are reviewed. The manufacturing problems encompass those of material quality, processing, and circuit design. In reality, these problems are closely related. Good substrates are a necessity for a reproducible process. The success of a particular circuit design approach is very much dependent on the limitations imposed by materials, processing capability and chip architecture. The manufacturing technology for fabricating GaAs monolithic microwave integrated circuits has improved over the past two years. The refinements now being made are directed primarily at enhancement of yield, realization of performance, and increase in circuit complexity. The purpose of this review paper is to (1) address the issues affecting the manufacture of GaAs MMICs and (2) present the industrial status (through an industrial data base) in addressing such issues as yield, throughput, design rules, chip architecture, reliability, design for yield and manufacturability, substrate qualification, choice of processing technology and current status of process related models and sensitivity analysis.

articleTitle: Investigation of Optimum Interchip Signal Transmission Protocols using GaAs ΒFL MSI Components with Various I/O Peripheries
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A team comprised of Mayo Foundation and Rockwell International has undertaken a study of optimum approaches to the interconnection of high clock rate GaAs components on a large circuit board, including the noise environment created thereby. We discuss the design constraints, fabrication, and measured results of two MSI-complexity GaAs integrated circuits, one synchronous and the other asynchronous, designed specifically to investigate the performance strengths and anomalies of interconnected GaAs digital devices.

articleTitle: Interface Reaction of SiO2 Encapsulant with GaAs Substrate and its Effect to FET Characteristics
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The interface layer between annealed GaAs and SiO<inf>2</inf> affects the device characteristics of Si-implanted GaAs FETs and their uniformity in the wafer. Photoluminescence and photocapacitance measurements show that the acceptor level with the activation energy of 0.08eV is introduced at the annealed surface. This acceptor is caused by the depletion of As atoms at the substrate surface, although SiO<inf>2</inf> encapsulant exists to prevent As evaporation. This is probably the same acceptor as that observed in bulk GaAs grown from Ga-rich melt. This acceptor compensates the implanted donor impurities and decreases their activation efficiency.

articleTitle: On the Design of MMICS
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A critical review will be made of the design approaches being used for MMICs by workers in the field. Following a brief description of the typical steps involved in the design and fabrication of an MMIC, the author will examine the design "philosophy" being used, in particular its limitations with regard to treatment of fabrication tolerances and circuit sensitivity to element values. The advantages and limitations of present CAD software will be addressed, and suggestions will be made for needed developments in device modeling and software for MMIC design requirements of the future.

articleTitle: A Microwave Photoconductance Technique for Non-Destructive Characterization of Semi-Insulating GaAs Substrates
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A microwave photoconductance technique for non-destructive characterization of electrical uniformity of semi-insulating GaAs substrates is presented, and applied to Cr-doped HB and undoped LEC substrates. A theoretical and experimental analysis shows that photoconductance is related to the effective lifetime of photo-generated electrons in both type of substrates. Photoconductance variation in Cr-doped substrates is less pronounced, and is related to Cr acceptor concentration. The photoconductance variation in undoped LEC substrates is more pronounced with U,M or W-shaped distribution, and reflects concentration fluctuation of residual acceptors such as carbon.

articleTitle: A Self-Aligned Gate Modolation-Doped (Al,Ga)As/GaAs FET IC Process
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A completely planar, self-aligned gate by ion implantation process for the fabrication of ultra-high speed ICs based on high performance, enhancement-mode (E-mode) modulation-doped (Al,Ga)As/GaAs FETs (MODFETs) has been developed. E-mode, self-aligned gate MODFETs have been fabricated with an extrinsic transconductance of 249 mS/mm and an output conductance below 10 mS/mm at room temperature. Ring oscillators utilizing direct-coupled FET logic (DCFL) gates have been measured at room temperature with a gate propagation delay as low as 17.6 ps/stage and a power dissipation of 2.65 mw/stage; a gate propagation delay of 24.3 ps/stage was obtained at 0.33 mW/stage for a delay-power product per stage of 8.2 fJ.

articleTitle: A Low Cost GaAs Monolithic Lna for TVRO Applications
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A low noise amplifier has been developed for the 3.7 to 4.2 GHz frequency band. This two stage amplifier chip provides 21.0 ± 1 dB gain and a 1.3 dB maximum noise figure across the design frequency band. The chip contains all the DC bias and most of the RF matching circuitry and is fabricated within a 22 × 35 mil<sup>2</sup> area. The amplifier input matching network is realized in external circuitry.

articleTitle: Growth and Characterization of Dislocation-Free GaAs Mixed Crystals for IC Substrates
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Semi-insulating GaAs single crystals mixed with In or InAs have been successfully grown dislocation-free (DF) by improving thermal and crystal growth conditions. The suitability of DF-GaAs for IC substrate was demonstrated by direct evaluation of the uniformity of FET arrays by ion implantation (I<sup>2</sup>). The average value of the threshold voltage of 625 FETs (gate length of 1µm and width of 5µm) of matrix arrays, each separated by 200µm, in 5mm squre region was -0.022V with standard deviation of 13mV which is much smaller than that in the conventional LEC crystals (50 ~ 100mV).

articleTitle: A Low Cost Multiport Microwave Package for GaAs ICS
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: This paper describes a multiport microwave chip carrier designed to solve the classical problems associated with packaging GaAs circuits with more than 2-4 I/O ports operating at GHz rates. The chip carrier contains nine copper/polyimide layers to provide 50-ohm stripline signal lines and a dedicated power plane. Chip capacitors located close to the IC serve to bypass two low Impedance power lines. Heat sinking is achieved by thermal conduction through copper heat columns under the IC. Initial testing and evaluation has yielded excellent results in RF performance, manufacturing yield and cost, solder reflow capability, and low failure rate under thermal cycling. The design of the package and test results are presented.

articleTitle: 20 and 30 GHz MMIC Technology for Future Space Communication Antenna Systems
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: The development of fully monolithic gallium arsenide (GaAs) receive and transmit modules is described. These modules are slated for phased array antenna applications in future 30/20 GHz communications satellite systems. Performance goals and various approaches to achieve them are briefly described. The latest design and performance results of components, submodules and modules are presented.

articleTitle: A 20 GHz 5-Bit Phase Shift Transmit Module with 16 dB Gain
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A fully monolithic transmit module chip operating over the 17.7-20.2 GHz band is described. This 6.3 × 4.7 mm MMIC contains five phase shifter bits, five gain stages and digital interface circuitry. An overall gain of 15 dB has been achieved at band center, with only ± 0.5 dB gain variation with changes in phase shifter state. Phase shifts are within 5° of the desired values. This MMIC represents the highest level of integration yet reported for circuits operating at 20 GHz.

articleTitle: 2 to 30 GHz Monolithic Distributed Amplifier
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: A low noise distributed amplifier is demonstrated over the 2 to 26.5 GHz band. The device exhibits a gain of 6 ± 0.3 dB over this band with a maximum noise figure of 5A dB and a maximum input/output VSWR of 1.7. The output power at the 1 dB gain compression point is typically 13 dBm. The 7-section distributed amplifier is fabricated on a chip with dimensions of 1.1×3.2 mm using optical lithography.

articleTitle: GaAs Surface Orientated Microwave Pin Diodes
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: This paper describes the design and fabrication techniques for successful realisation of two types of GaAs PIN diodes which lend themselves to integration into GaAs ICs. PIN diodes with a new shallow trench structure exhibit superior microwave, performance to the interdigitated structure.

articleTitle: Microwave Frequency GaAs Charge-Coupled Devices
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Operation of GaAs CCDs up to 4.2 GHz is reported here. Measurements of charge transfer efficiency at 2.5 GHz have shown it to be well in excess 0.99 per transfer. With the recent success of full incorporation of high speed CCDs in GaAs ICs to form a monolithic transversal filter operating at 1 GHz, there has been a strong effort to investigate the high frequency limits of the device and to characterize those limits in terms of materials technology and design criteria. Our results are now approaching the fundamental physical limitations imposed by the device structure and material parameters.

articleTitle: 3-Stage Wideband RLC Feedback GaAs Monolithic Amplifier
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: This paper describes the design, fabrication and performance of one, two and three-stage GaAs monolithic RLC feedback amplifiers. All amplifiers were self-biased and required only one supply. The fabrication process uses two dielectrics, polyimide and silicon nitride, to achieve low capacitance metal crossovers and high capacitance per unit area capacitors. The amplifiers had gains of 8 dB/stage with a 3 dB cut-off frequency of 4 GHz for the single stage, and 3 GHz for the two and three-stage amplifiers.

articleTitle: Advanced GaAs DCFL Constructions with 8 × 8 BIT Parallel Moltipliers
publicationTitle: 1984 IEEE GaAs IC Symposium Technical Digest
abstract: Three types of GaAs 8x8 bit parallel multipliers were developed using the array multiplier architecture, and they were compared to each other in their properties. They were different only in the circuits of the adders. Type I consists of NOR gates and the gate widths of FETs are constant. Type II consists of NOR gates and the "effective" fanout is kept constant to 2.4 by the modification of FET gate widths. Type III consists of complexed gates (AND-NOR, OR-AND-NOR). By using high purity MO—substrates and applying self-alignment technique with W-Al gate in the FET fabrication process, the high yield of more than 15 % was obtained for these multipliers. The multiply time of type II was 20% faster than that of type I.
